summary:
Muş province stands under the national framework of Türkiye. No Muş-specific ordinance, incident or court decision is documented for the province, so what a trans visitor faces in Muş is what the national sources record for the country as a whole.

The baseline is permissive in narrow terms and hostile in every operative one. Homosexuality has not been a criminal offence since the Ottoman penal code of 1858, and legal gender recognition has been available since 1988, but no comprehensive law prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, and same-sex marriage is not recognised. A visitor's partner, marriage or transition status therefore carries no protective weight in dealings with Turkish authorities.

Criminalisation is pending rather than enacted, and the distinction has not slowed enforcement. Human Rights Watch reported on 29 October 2025 that a leaked draft judicial-reform package, the 11th Judicial Reform, would pave the way for criminal charges against LGBT people and described it as one of the most alarming rights rollbacks in decades; activists held a press conference in Istanbul on 28 October 2025 against the provisions targeting LGBT people. Amnesty International records three draft law packages targeting LGBT people made public during 2025, an unprecedented assault that would criminalise expression of LGBT identities and consensual same-sex relations and make legal gender recognition nearly impossible. None of the three was submitted to parliament.

Assembly is the sharpest street-level exposure. Since 2015 local authorities have repeatedly banned and forcibly dispersed Pride marches, with police using water cannon and tear gas against participants in the 2015 and 2016 Istanbul parades. In June 2025 authorities issued blanket bans against the Istanbul LGBTI and Trans pride marches, police subjected peaceful protesters to unlawful use of force, over 90 people were arbitrarily detained, and prosecutions of 92 people for participating in pride marches were still running at the end of the year.

The parent framework also governs the interactions most likely to occur on a visit. Foreign nationals are required to produce original photo identification at transit checkpoints, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira and formal warnings of detention for non-compliance, and police continue to conduct "General Information Gathering" (GBT) identity checks in which trans women have been held and documented without charge. Any such stop compares a visitor's documents against their presentation. Trans prisoners are placed according to registered sex, and a Health Ministry regulation reported in September 2025 barred hospitals from recording the "other" option in gender-related medical-board e-reports, tightening the official record around trans patients.
tangentialFactors:
The documented enforcement examples come from other provinces, which is how the national pattern is evidenced rather than a sign that Muş is exempt. Istanbul supplies the Pride bans, the mass detentions and the street-level GBT stops; an İzmir court supplies the December 2025 dissolution of the Young LGBTI+ Association, ruling that it had shared "obscene" images incompatible with "society's moral values" that could "encourage or promote" LGBTI identities. Muş has no counter-evidence of its own, and absence of provincial records is not evidence of provincial tolerance.

There is a consistent gap between what is proposed and what is applied. Three draft packages circulated in 2025 without reaching parliament, and press reports in early 2026 stated that the government was considering legislation criminalising public advocacy of "behaviour contrary to biological sex" — a provision ultimately not included in that year's judicial reform package. The legislative output is unfinished; the policing, the bans and the prosecutions are not.

The decriminalisation dates are old enough to be misleading on their own. A penal code of 1858 and gender recognition in 1988 sit alongside a 2025 in which three separate draft laws targeted LGBT people in one year and Pride participants were prosecuted into the following year. The direction of travel is the relevant fact for a visitor, not the age of the statute that decriminalised.
localsOnly:
Openly LGBTI people are barred from military service. Conscripts who declare their homosexuality are classified under a definition of homosexuality as a "psychosexual illness", must provide photographic proof of their orientation, and risk their "unfit report" being leaked publicly. This bears on residents and returning nationals rather than short-term visitors.

Legal gender recognition has been available in Türkiye since 1988, but the three draft packages published during 2025 would have made it nearly impossible, and the September 2025 Health Ministry regulation requires gender-related medical-board reports to be issued as e-reports with the "other" option barred, following a Kayseri Provincial Health Directorate circular that added "gender reassignment" as an official report reason. The change risks profiling trans patients in official records.

There is no comprehensive law prohibiting discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, and same-sex marriage is not recognised, so employment, housing, healthcare and family claims have no statutory footing. Organisational space is contracting: an İzmir court ordered the dissolution of the Young LGBTI+ Association in December 2025, and Pride marches have been banned and dispersed by force since 2015, with over 90 people arbitrarily detained in June 2025 and prosecutions of 92 participants continuing at year's end.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Muş-specific incident, police practice, local ordinance or court decision is sourced for the province. The provincial assessment is derived entirely from national reporting, and whether any local deviation exists in either direction is unresolved on the available material.

The legislative position is unsettled. The 11th Judicial Reform package leaked in October 2025 and the two other draft packages published during 2025 were not submitted to parliament, and press reports in early 2026 on criminalising public advocacy of "behaviour contrary to biological sex" state that the provision was ultimately not included in that year's package. Whether any of these measures has since been reintroduced, rewritten or abandoned is not sourced here.

The status of the June 2025 Pride prosecutions in Türkiye — whether the 92 cases resulted in convictions, were dropped or remain pending — is not stated in the available sources beyond their continuation at the end of 2025. The same is true of the outcome demanded by rights groups following the death of the trans prisoner Poyraz at Sincan Women's Prison on 1 December 2025: an independent investigation was sought, and no result is recorded.
